theme: Sing a new song; let everything that has breath praise
readingInstruction: Read Psalms 149 and 150. These are the final two psalms in the Psalter, and they close the book with praise. You will read them again in Unit 24. Read them now as the response to Esther’s deliverance and the dedication of the wall.
settingTheScene: Psalm 149 calls the people to sing a new song, with dancing and with a two-edged sword in hand. Psalm 150 is the grand finale, naming where, why, and with what to praise God. The Psalter began with Psalm 1, the blessed man who meditates on the law. It ends with every breath praising the LORD.
observation: “Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise in the assembly of the godly!” (149:1).
“Let Israel be glad in his Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King!” (149:2).
“For the LORD takes pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble with salvation” (149:4).
“Let the high praises of God be in their throats and two-edged swords in their hands” (149:6).
“This is honor for all his godly ones. Praise the LORD!” (149:9).
“Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens!” (150:1).
“Praise him for his mighty deeds; praise him according to his excellent greatness!” (150:2).
“Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Praise the LORD!” (150:6).
interpretation:
Psalm 149 begins with a new song. Throughout the Psalms, a “new song” is sung when God does something new. For the returned community, it means the new thing God has done in bringing them back, rebuilding, and keeping them safe. Praise includes dancing and music with tambourine and lyre.

Verse 4 is wonderful: “The LORD takes pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble with salvation.” God is not only worshiped but delights in the worshipers. The humble, those who do not rely on themselves, are crowned with salvation.

Then the psalm takes a surprising turn: “two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance on the nations.” This has been read in many ways. In its Old Testament setting, it refers to God’s people participating in his justice. The people of God are not passive. In the New Testament, the sword of the Spirit is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17; Hebrews 4:12). The final victory belongs to the Lord, and his people stand with him.

Psalm 150 is the climax. It answers four questions. Where? In his sanctuary and in the mighty heavens, which is everywhere. Why? For his mighty deeds and his excellent greatness. How? With trumpet, harp, lyre, tambourine, strings, pipe, and loud clashing cymbals. Praise is wholehearted and full of sound. Who? “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.” That includes you.

The five books of the Psalter each end with a doxology, and the fifth book ends with this final one that is itself the doxology of the whole. After 150 psalms of laments, confessions, complaints, and hope, the book ends in praise. It tells us where all prayer is meant to end.
connection: Ephesians 6:17 identifies the sword of the Spirit as the word of God. Hebrews 4:12: “The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword.” Revelation 5:9 speaks of the new song sung to the Lamb. Colossians 3:16 says to sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with thankfulness. Luke 19:40: if the people were silent, the stones would cry out. Revelation 19:1-6 is the hallelujah of the multitude.
application:
Use Psalm 150 as a morning prayer for a week. Praise with your breath, your voice, and your body.

Sing or listen to a hymn or song that is new to you.

Ask: where is God doing something new that deserves a new song?
prayerPrompts: Sing or speak a new song to God, and let it be yours.
Thank him that he takes pleasure in his people.
Let everything that has breath praise him, and add your own.
